Observation During Mixing
A white precipitate of barium sulphate forms instantly. A clear chemical reaction has taken place!
Mass of Reactants = Mass of Products
Law of Conservation of Mass
Mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. The total mass of the reactants is always equal to the total mass of the products.
Barium chloride + Sodium sulphate -> Barium sulphate + Sodium chloride
Wood + Oxygen consumed = Ash + Carbon dioxide gas + Water vapour
Atomic View: Why Mass Is Conserved
Law of Conservation of Mass: Matter changes form, but its total quantity is forever preserved.

elements.text: Total number of each type of atom before reaction = Total number after reaction.

beats.narration: Think about a heavy wooden log burning in a fireplace.
When the fire dies down, all you have left is a tiny handful of grey ash.
It feels like over nine kilograms of matter simply vanished into thin air!
On the other hand, take a shiny iron nail left outside in the rain.
Over weeks, it gets covered in thick rust, and when you weigh it, the rusted nail is actually heavier than the original nail!
Did mass get destroyed in the fire, and magically created in the rust?
For centuries, people thought matter could appear and disappear. Let us see why that was a mistake.
To find the truth, French scientist Antoine Lavoisier realized we must trap everything inside a sealed container.
Here is a conical flask containing sodium sulphate solution, marked as solution Y.
Suspended carefully inside is a tiny ignition tube holding barium chloride solution, our solution X.
A thin thread holds the tube upright so the two liquids do not touch each other yet.
We place this entire undisturbed setup on a sensitive digital balance and note down the reading.
Now, tilt and swirl the flask so that solution X spills into solution Y.
New substances have formed. Now we put the sealed flask back on the weighing balance.
What do you think the reading shows? Exactly 300.25 grams! Not a single milligram was lost or gained.
This leads us to the foundational law of all chemistry: The Law of Conservation of Mass.
Let us write down the word equation to see both sides clearly.
Now we can explain our burning log: if you capture the smoke, water vapour, and carbon dioxide produced, their mass plus the ash exactly equals the original wood plus the oxygen consumed!
Why does mass stay identical during a reaction? John Dalton gave us the answer.
A chemical reaction is simply a rearrangement of atoms. No atom is ever created, and no atom is ever destroyed.
Every single atom present on the left side is still there on the right side, just bonded to different partners.
Because every atom has a fixed mass, and all the atoms are accounted for, the total mass before and after reaction must remain unchanged.
